title: Classical algorithms for sparse random Hamiltonians via free probability
authors: Matthew Ding, Robbie King, Thomas Schuster
problem: The sparse random Pauli model, a sum of \(m=\mathrm{poly}(n)\) random \(n\)-qubit Pauli strings with random signs, was proposed by Chen and coauthors as a candidate for average-case quantum advantage in many-body simulation. It looks hard classically: it scrambles, has a sign problem and grows entanglement quickly, and its instance-to-instance fluctuations are large enough for a quantum computer to resolve. Can a classical algorithm compute its spectral, thermal and dynamical properties as efficiently as a quantum simulation?
result: Yes, with high probability over the instance. For \(m=\Omega(n^3)\), times and inverse temperatures up to \(o(n/\log n)\), and accuracy \(\varepsilon\) down to \(2^{-o(n/\log n)}\), the spectral amplitude, partition function, thermal expectation values, and time-ordered and out-of-time-order correlators can be computed classically in time \((1/\varepsilon)^{2+o(1)}(n/\delta)\,\mathrm{poly}(t,\beta)\). A variant handles the model with an added Pauli spike at its spectral phase transition in the same time.
significance: The result removes a leading proposal for scalable average-case quantum advantage in Hamiltonian simulation, leaving at most the quadratic speedup in \(1/\varepsilon\) from amplitude estimation. It also identifies a mechanism, exponential concentration of free cumulants, by which an average-case problem with large fluctuations can still be classically easy, a test any new proposal of this kind will need to pass.
limitations: The model is fully non-local, so the result does not cover local Hamiltonians of physical interest. Beyond times of order \(n/\log n\), or at precisions exponentially small in \(n\), the expansion breaks down and a polynomial quantum advantage remains possible. The assumption \(m=\Omega(n^3)\) can be relaxed to \(m=\Omega(n)\) only under a combinatorial conjecture. The authors state that the main ideas were developed without AI one to two years ago; ChatGPT 5.6 and 6 Pro were later used to extend the results, including the step from cube-root to near-linear times and the idea of using operator-valued free probability for one part, and Codex for numerics.
summary_basis: Description based on the full arXiv HTML of v1, read 2026-11-28: Secs. 1–3 (model, Theorems 1–2, Table 1, the loop-free approximation, the free cumulant expansion of Eqs. (6)–(12), the algorithm and its error bound (13)) and the AI statement; the appendices with the coding-theory and cumulant proofs were read in outline. Editorial checks: on a random instance with n = 10, m = 40 and distinct Pauli strings, the second moment is exactly 1 and the fourth moment equals 2 + c − 1/m to machine precision, with c the crossing term of Eq. (5); on an instance with n = 10, m = 60, keeping free cumulants through order 4 reproduces the 10th, 16th and 24th moments to relative errors 4 × 10^-4, 3 × 10^-3 and 1 × 10^-2, against 17%, 37% and 72% for the semicircle alone. At this small n the higher cumulants do not decay monotonically, consistent with the paper's restriction to orders below about n/log n.

methods_basis: Based on the linked paper version. Derivations marked as editorial, and suggested uses in other problems, are editorial guidance rather than results of the paper.
description: The Hamiltonian is \(H=m^{-1/2}\sum_{i=1}^mJ_iP_i\) with \(J_i=\pm1\) and \(P_i\) uniformly random Pauli strings. With exponentially many terms it would be a GUE matrix with a semicircle spectrum; with polynomially many it inherits the semicircle and the signatures of chaos but carries \(O(1/m)\) corrections that depend on which strings were drawn. Those corrections are the target: computing them for a given instance is a well-defined average-case problem.

Every property considered reduces to moments \(\overline{\mathrm{Tr}}(H^k)=2^{-n}\tr H^k\), through Taylor expansion of \(e^{-iHt}\) or \(e^{-\beta H}\). A moment is a sum over \(m^k\) index strings, but for random Paulis the only nonzero traces come, with probability \(1-2^{-\Omega(n)}\), from partitions of the \(k\) positions into even blocks, as long as \(k\le\gamma n/\log n\). The proof uses coding theory to exclude short loops of Pauli strings multiplying to the identity.

The partitions are then grouped by free cumulants. Non-crossing pairings alone give the semicircle; the \(k\)-th free cumulant collects the connected diagrams, which are averages of many random signs or involve index collisions, and the paper proves \(|\kappa_k|=O(\delta^{-1/2}(Ck/m)^{k/4})\) with probability \(1-\delta\). The algorithm computes the first \(\ell\approx\log(1/\varepsilon)/\log m\) moments exactly by expanding \(H^{\ell/2}\) in the Pauli basis, converts them to free cumulants, sets the higher cumulants to zero, and rebuilds all moments up to order \(L\approx\log(1/\varepsilon)+t\) through the moment–cumulant relation.

The error is \(O\bigl(\delta^{-1/2}[C(\ell+2)/m]^{(\ell+2)/4}+(2et/L)^L\bigr)\), and the dominant cost is \(O(n\,m^{\ell/2})\), which gives the \((1/\varepsilon)^{2+O(1/\log m)}\) runtime. Correlators require operator-valued free probability, and the spiked model, whose spectrum develops a cube-root cusp at \(\lambda=1\), requires a more general expansion; neither raises the cost. The authors note the matching \(1/\varepsilon^2\) scaling of a quantum simulation that estimates the same quantities by sampling.

methods.technique: Loop-free diagrammatic decomposition for a single instance
methods.explanation: Diagrammatic expansions usually require averaging over disorder. Here one needs exact statements for one fixed draw of Pauli strings. The obstacle is accidental products of a few strings that equal the identity, which would create extra terms; random strings avoid them at the relevant lengths.
math: Write \(\overline{\mathrm{Tr}}(H^k)=m^{-k/2}\sum_{i_1,\ldots,i_k}J_{i_1}\cdots J_{i_k}\overline{\mathrm{Tr}}(P_{i_1}\cdots P_{i_k})\). If the strings are distinct, the second moment is exactly \(1\). For the fourth moment, if no four distinct strings multiply to the identity, \[\overline{\mathrm{Tr}}(H^4)=2+\frac1{m^2}\sum_{i\ne j}s_{ij}-\frac1m,\] where \(s_{ij}=\pm1\) records whether \(P_i\) and \(P_j\) commute. The two non-crossing pairings give \(2\), the crossing pairing gives the sum, and the all-equal term corrects double counting.

The crossing sum is an average of \(m(m-1)\) signs that are equally likely to be \(\pm1\), so it has mean zero and size \(O(1/m)\); it is the fourth free cumulant up to the collision term. Editorial check: on a random instance with \(n=10\), \(m=40\), the exact fourth moment and the right-hand side agree to machine precision (both \(1.92\)). For general \(k\), the paper shows that no loop with an odd number of any string occurs up to \(k\le\gamma n/\log n\), so the decomposition over even-block partitions, Eq. (6), is exact there with probability \(1-2^{-\alpha n}\).
methods.transfer: Any random-operator model whose terms are drawn from a large group with few short relations, such as random Clifford or random fermionic monomials, admits the same instance-wise reduction to partitions.

methods.explanation: The number of diagrams explodes with the order, so exact moments of high order are out of reach. Free cumulants package the diagrams so that the low ones carry nearly all the instance-dependent information; the rest can be dropped with a controlled error.
math: Moments and free cumulants are related by a sum over non-crossing partitions, \[\overline{\mathrm{Tr}}(H^k)=\sum_{\pi\in NC(k)}\prod_{V\in\pi}\kappa_{|V|}(H),\] which can be inverted recursively. Keeping only \(\kappa_2=1\) gives the Catalan numbers, the moments of the semicircle. A connected diagram of order \(k\) built from \(k/2\) crossing pairings averages \(O(m^{k/2})\) random signs, so its size is \(O(m^{-k/4})\), while every collision costs a further factor \(1/m\). The proved bound \(|\kappa_k|\le O(\delta^{-1/2}(Ck/m)^{k/4})\) makes the truncation error at order \(\ell\) of size \((C\ell/m)^{\ell/4}\).

Editorial check: for an instance with \(n=10\), \(m=60\), keeping \(\kappa_2\) and \(\kappa_4\) and rebuilding the moments reproduces \(\overline{\mathrm{Tr}}(H^{10})\approx35.97\) to relative error \(4\times10^{-4}\), whereas the semicircle predicts \(42\). At such small \(n\), \(\kappa_8\) is not smaller than \(\kappa_6\), as expected when \(k\) exceeds the loop-free range.
methods.transfer: Expanding around a free-probability limit and correcting with a few cumulants is a general strategy for average-case dequantization; it applies wherever the limiting object is free and the corrections concentrate, for example random-circuit correlators.
